reference.source: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry; DSM-5-TR
clinicalPearls: A chronic psychotic disorder defined by a combination of positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech and behaviour) and negative symptoms (blunted affect, avolition, social withdrawal), with significant functional decline
Diagnosis requires continuous disturbance over an extended period (on the order of six months) with an active phase of characteristic symptoms, after excluding mood and substance-related causes
Onset is typically in late adolescence or early adulthood, often somewhat earlier and with poorer premorbid function in men
Cognitive impairment (attention, working memory, executive function) is a core feature and a major driver of disability
Antipsychotic medication is the cornerstone of treatment, described here as a principle; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness and requires haematological monitoring
Comprehensive care combines pharmacotherapy with psychosocial interventions, family education, supported employment, and relapse prevention
Suicide risk is elevated, particularly early in the illness and in those with insight into their deterioration
Duration of untreated psychosis affects outcome, so early recognition and intervention are important
reference.pathophysiology: Schizophrenia is a neurodevelopmental disorder with strong genetic contribution in which aberrant dopaminergic signalling (mesolimbic overactivity linked to positive symptoms and mesocortical hypofunction linked to negative and cognitive symptoms) interacts with glutamatergic and other neurotransmitter abnormalities. Structural and functional brain changes, synaptic pruning abnormalities, and gene-environment interactions such as obstetric complications and cannabis exposure contribute to the emergence of illness.
additionalDifferentials: Bipolar disorder or major depression with psychotic features
Brief psychotic disorder and schizophreniform disorder
Psychosis secondary to a medical or neurological condition
Autoimmune or paraneoplastic encephalitis presenting with psychosis
additionalInvestigations: Substance use screening including cannabis and stimulants
Neuroimaging and, where indicated, investigation for organic or autoimmune causes in first-episode psychosis
Baseline metabolic parameters (weight, glucose, lipids) and ECG before and during antipsychotic treatment
Full blood count monitoring during clozapine treatment
Cognitive assessment to characterise functional impairment
redFlags: Command hallucinations or suicidal ideation with risk to self
Delusional beliefs that place others at risk
First-episode psychosis with atypical features suggesting an organic cause
Signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome such as rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability
reference.prognosis: Schizophrenia usually follows a chronic course with episodic exacerbations and variable residual impairment. Better outcomes are associated with acute onset, good premorbid functioning, prominent mood symptoms, and early treatment, whereas insidious onset, prominent negative symptoms, and long untreated psychosis predict poorer functional recovery.
pitfalls: Attributing first-episode psychosis to a primary psychiatric disorder without excluding organic and substance causes
Neglecting metabolic monitoring in patients on antipsychotics
Delaying a clozapine trial in genuinely treatment-resistant illness
Underestimating suicide risk, especially early in the course
Focusing only on positive symptoms while ignoring disabling negative and cognitive symptoms
